gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1020t:
Health checks for people caught in the World Trade Center attack anchor GAO-05-1020T, a statement dated September 10, 2005. Nearly 3,000 people died in the 2001 attack. About 40,000 responders faced dust, smoke, and stress at the site. Federal funds back a set of screening and follow-up health plans.

GAO weighed how those plans had moved ahead. It looked at plans run by state, city, and private groups. It also looked at federal plans for federal workers who served at the site. Those plans lagged, the title warns. Lessons from the whole set close the review, for use in the next mass disaster.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1050t:
Army Corps of Engineers, GAO-05-1050T of September 28, 2005, gives the past record of the levee plan that failed New Orleans in Hurricane Katrina. Surge water can top 20 feet on the Gulf and Atlantic coasts. The Lake Pontchartrain and Vicinity project, first cleared in 1965, was built to shield the city's lowlands from such surges and storm rain.

Katrina's surge broke levees that form part of that plan and flooded much of the city. GAO sets out what the project was meant to do and how it grew. It then traces the cash the project drew over time. No fixes are urged here; the facts frame the next fight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-350t:
GAO's 2005 High-Risk Update, GAO-05-350T of February 17, 2005, is the roll call of federal work most prone to waste and fraud. Since 1990, GAO has kept such a list for each new Congress. This round speaks to the 109th Congress. It tells the state of each field flagged in 2003. It names new fields that earn the flag.

Some flags mark cash risk in set plans. Some mark vast change tasks the state must get right. Fixes could save billions of dollars, lift service, and mend trust in how the state keeps its vows. The list aims the eyes of Congress and the White House.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-360t:
Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, GAO-05-360T of March 2, 2005, warns that the pension backstop's own frame leaves it bare to risk. More than 34 million workers and the retired in about 30,000 work plans lean on its cover. In July 2003, GAO put that cover plan on its high-risk list. In fiscal year 2004, it lost a net $12.1 billion. Its hole grew to $23.3 billion.

Thin funds in work plans topped $450 billion at that year's end. GAO names the frame flaws that curb the backstop's shield. It tells what steps the backstop takes to see and steer the risks it bears.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-390t:
Tactical Aircraft, GAO-05-390T of March 3, 2005, previews two full grades of the Pentagon's twin jet paths. The F/A-22 and the Joint Strike Fighter would take the place of old jets with stealth craft. Their joint bill for years to come tops $240 billion. Each path has hit slips in cost and time since its birth. Full tales were due later that month.

The facts here lift the chief fears in each build. It asks what those fears mean for the whole bid to renew the war fleet. If both jets lag, old jets must fly past their years, or gaps yawn in the sky guard.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-400t:
Army National Guard, GAO-05-400T of March 16, 2005, tells how a paper-bound travel pay path fails troops called to war. Call-ups surged for the war on terror. Guard troops who roam for duty must file forms to get their road cash back. The path crawls and errs. Late or lost pay hits troops and their homes, who may front cash they can ill spare.

GAO lays out the harm in full. It grades the checks on the path, its staff, and its tools. It asks if the Pentagon's bid to run the path by wire will cure the flaws. It lists more acts to make pay true and swift.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-440t:
The system that tracks foreign students in the United States is reviewed in GAO testimony GAO-05-440T, given on March 17, 2005. The Student and Exchange Visitor Information System, run by the Department of Homeland Security, records data on students and exchange visitors before and during their stay. Early use brought many complaints from schools. Congress asked GAO to report on how the system was now working.

Signs pointed to steady gains in system performance. Fewer fixes were being requested, and school groups said the system worked better than in its first year. The department had added software updates and more Help Desk staff. But some core performance needs were not being formally measured. Help Desk problems still caused hardship for students. Fee collection worries had eased since the prior year. The testimony weighs the gains against the gaps that remained.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-450t:
Cleanup and reuse of brownfield sites is covered in testimony GAO-05-450T, dated April 5, 2005. Brownfields are properties whose reuse may be blocked by the threat of pollution. The Environmental Protection Agency gives grants for site checks, job training, loans, and cleanups. GAO asked grant users, state officials, developers, and others what the program achieved and what more could be done.

Stakeholders said EPA funds cover early steps that other lenders often avoid, such as finding pollution and cleaning sites. In 10 states, officials said EPA help was key to building their own cleanup programs. EPA's measures covered some results but not progress on cleanup and reuse. Measures of health and environmental gains were also missing. That limited the ability of EPA and Congress to judge the program. The testimony records both praise for the grants and ideas to add to them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-520t:
The Defense Department's high-risk business areas are the theme of testimony GAO-05-520T, presented on April 13, 2005. GAO's 2005 high-risk list holds 25 areas across government. Eight of them sit inside the Defense Department. The department shares blame for six more that span government. GAO set out the list, flagged a growing worry about risk management, and named steps that could drive real reform.

The eight areas touch nearly every part of defense business. They include buying weapons, managing contracts, running supply chains, and keeping the books. Two areas were new in 2005: the department's whole approach to business change, and its personnel security clearance program. GAO said these flaws waste billions of dollars each year. Senior leaders voiced strong support for reform. Yet GAO saw little hard proof of gains so far. It argued that deep change needs sound strategy, steady leadership, and a chief management official to own the work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-530t:
Federal grants that equip local first responders are tracked in testimony GAO-05-530T, presented on April 12, 2005. From fiscal year 2002 through 2005, the Office for Domestic Preparedness managed about $10.5 billion in grants. Most money flowed through a state grant program and an urban areas program. GAO described how awards are made, how fast funds move, and how recipients answer for results.

The office set rules for how states apply and how funds may be spent. It left states some choice in passing money down and buying gear. Congress and the office set time limits to speed awards. Even so, state and local buying rules could add months before gear arrived. Some states changed their buying steps to move faster. The office worked to sharpen state plans and checks on spending. GAO said the drive for accountability was still taking shape. Speed and control had to be built together.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-550t:
Privatizing the Intelsat satellite system under a 2000 law is reviewed in testimony GAO-05-550T, given on April 14, 2005. Intelsat began as a body owned by many nations and shielded from rivals. The ORBIT Act ordered its move to private hands to open the world satellite market. GAO traced why the change was sought, how far it has gone, and whether access to foreign markets has improved.

By the 1980s, private firms could compete for global satellite services. Intelsat's state-backed status still gave it an edge over new firms.  The shift took place in July 2001. The Federal Communications Commission found the plan met the act's terms. It let the private firm use its U.S. licenses while a public stock sale was pending. A 2004 law then let Intelsat skip that sale if it met set conditions. The testimony weighs how much of the act's promise has been kept.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-620t:
Working past the usual retirement age is the theme of GAO testimony GAO-05-620T, dated April 27, 2005. The first baby boomers reach Social Security age in 2008. As they retire, the worker base shrinks and health and pension costs climb. GAO says growth alone cannot close the budget gap. Keeping willing older staff on the job is one part of the answer.

Choice turns on health, pension and Social Security rules, and the need for cover for medical costs. A spouse's job and the supply of part-time or flexible work matter too. The statement lays out the trends and the levers for the Senate aging panel.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-760t:
Flu pandemic readiness is the focus of testimony GAO-05-760T, given May 26, 2005. Vaccine shortages in the 2004-2005 season raised fears about a worldwide outbreak. Experts warned that bird flu in Asia could spark one. One federal estimate put U.S. deaths at 89,000 to 207,000. Illnesses could reach 38 million to 89 million. GAO spoke to disease tracking and to gaps in planning.

The testimony rests on GAO work going back to 2000, plus fresh checks in May 2005. GAO traced the systems meant to spot and track a pandemic early. It also laid out concerns about vaccine supply and response plans. Its core message matches its title: challenges remain in preparedness. The record shows where federal plans still fall short.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-810t:
Pension reform abroad is the subject of testimony GAO-05-810T, delivered June 16, 2005. Worker-to-retiree ratios are falling in most rich nations. That strains pension systems where today's workers fund today's payouts. The U.S. system faces the same long-term squeeze, though a milder one. A House panel asked GAO for early lessons from nations that have already reformed.

GAO found that all the nations studied have reformed in some way. Nearly all cut benefits. Most also raised payments into the system, often by raising retirement ages. Shielding low-income groups was common, though it can dull work incentives. Nations with reserve funds teach the value of early action and clean governance. Funds kept apart from other budget needs hold up best, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-830t:
A call to remake government fills testimony GAO-05-830T, delivered July 13, 2005. GAO argues the nation faces deep 21st century tests. Long-term fiscal strain leads the list. Security threats shift, the economy links worldwide, and health costs climb. The testimony makes the case for change. It then shows how agencies can become high-performing bodies. It closes with paths that support the remake.

GAO said the nation is on an imprudent and unsustainable fiscal path. Known age trends and rising health costs drive the gap. Treating every old program as a given will not work, GAO held. Agencies must reexamine their base of programs and tax rules. They must also build results-focused cultures. The testimony frames that shift as the price of meeting new demands.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-840t:
Radiation detectors against nuclear smuggling are covered in testimony GAO-05-840T, given June 21, 2005. A UN agency counted 650 confirmed trafficking cases from 1993 to 2004. Much of the material could feed a bomb or a dirty bomb. GAO summed up its past reports on U.S. detector work at home and abroad. It named the agencies in charge, their coordination flaws, and how well the gear works.

Four agencies run these programs. Congress gave about $800 million from fiscal years 1994 through 2005. About $500 million went to work abroad, and about $300 million to U.S. entry points. A border program placed gear at 66 sites, mostly in Russia, by the end of fiscal year 2004. Over 470 portal monitors stood at U.S. sites by May 2005.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-850t:
Medicaid drug rebates are questioned in testimony GAO-05-850T, delivered June 22, 2005. Drug makers pay rebates to states to curb Medicaid drug costs. The rebates rest on two prices makers report: best price and average maker price. The testimony rests on a February 2005 GAO report on the program. That report's title states the core concern plainly.

For the report, GAO reviewed program guidance and inspector general findings. It analyzed rebates for brand name drugs. Its verdict was that oversight is inadequate. That gap raises concerns about whether rebates paid to states are right. The testimony brings the report's case to Congress in short form. It shows how weak checks on reported prices can ripple into state payments.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-880t:
The securities regulator's first audit is reported in testimony GAO-05-880T, delivered July 27, 2005. A 2002 law made the Securities and Exchange Commission file audited accounts. GAO agreed to run the first audit, for fiscal year 2004. It judged whether the accounts were reliable. It also judged internal controls and legal compliance. The testimony presents a May 2005 GAO report.

GAO gave the accounts a clean opinion. They fairly showed the agency's position as of September 30, 2004. But GAO gave an adverse opinion on internal controls. Material weaknesses hit how accounts are prepared, how penalties and disgorgements are recorded, and information security. Controls over legal compliance were effective, GAO found. It found no reportable breaches of the laws it tested.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-910t:
A second update on the Capitol Visitor Center is testimony GAO-05-910T, delivered July 14, 2005. Congress last heard on the project on June 14. The Architect of the Capitol runs the build with a construction manager. GAO reviewed schedules and money reports, watched work at the site, and spoke with staff and fire officials. It did not perform an audit, GAO noted.

The testimony reports progress on set milestones in the month since the last hearing. It covers how the schedule is being managed day to day. It also lays out project costs and funding. A key thread is what schedule slips could do to the final bill. The update gives Congress a fresh, dated snapshot for its oversight of the long-running build.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1000t:
Ways to shrink the tax gap fill testimony GAO-06-1000T, delivered July 26, 2006. The gap is what taxpayers owe but do not pay on time by choice. For tax year 2001, the gross gap was put at $345 billion. Officials expect to recover $55 billion of it. That leaves a net gap of $290 billion. Each 1 percent cut in the net gap would yield about $3 billion a year.

GAO, drawing on prior work, weighed three broad approaches. One simplifies or reforms the tax system itself. One gives the tax service more enforcement tools. One gives it more enforcement resources. The testimony also lays out factors to guide a strategy that mixes the three. When some taxpayers do not comply, GAO noted, the burden shifts to those who do.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1090t:
Risks in the Visa Waiver Program are the subject of GAO testimony delivered on September 7, 2006. The program lets citizens of 27 countries visit for 90 days or less without a visa. In fiscal year 2005, nearly 16 million people entered this way. After the September 11 attacks, fears grew that hostile actors could abuse the program. GAO met embassy officials in six member countries and reviewed risk checks.

The program eases travel, but stolen passports from member states are prized by criminals and terrorists. Border staff may lack time for deep checks. GAO found the Department of Homeland Security's risk review process weak. Key partners were not consulted, standards were unclear, and reports ran late. The tracking unit lacked staff to do its job. GAO urged more resources and firm rules for reporting lost passports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1100t:
Planning for a major Internet failure is the topic of GAO-06-1100T, testimony given on September 13, 2006. Most Internet infrastructure is owned by private firms, not the government. Federal policy charges the Department of Homeland Security with building a joint public and private recovery plan. GAO summed up its June 2006 report on that task. The report covered past disruptions, the laws that govern recovery, and the hurdles a joint plan faces.

Past events, such as Hurricane Katrina, caused local outages but no national collapse. Laws on infrastructure and disaster aid give broad guidance, yet roles for Internet recovery stay unclear. DHS had launched working groups and response drills, but its plans were partial and lacked time frames. GAO listed five hurdles, from the Internet's open design to private firms' reluctance to share data. It also cited weak agreement on when DHS should step in.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1110t:
The Next Generation Nuclear Plant, an advanced reactor project, is reviewed in GAO-06-1110T, testimony from September 2006. The Department of Energy began the project in 2003. The plant would make electricity and also supply heat to produce hydrogen for fuel cells. The Energy Policy Act of 2005 set a 2021 deadline for design and construction. GAO summed up a report issued the same day. It covered the project's schedule progress and DOE's path to commercial use.

GAO found the project still at an early stage. DOE had made initial progress toward near-term milestones. It was also chasing a more advanced technical approach than first planned. That choice raised fresh questions about cost, timing, and industry interest. The testimony draws on DOE research plans, two independent project reviews, and talks with regulators and industry staff.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1130t:
Contract management in the rebuilding of Iraq is assessed in GAO-06-1130T, testimony presented on September 28, 2006. The United States and its partners face a vast task: steadying and rebuilding a country at war. The Department of Defense runs a large share of the construction work. GAO drew on its own reviews and on work by the Special Inspector General for Iraq Reconstruction. It described both the progress made and the contract problems that slowed it.

Many projects fell short of hopes. Costs rose, schedules slipped, scopes shrank, and some projects were cancelled outright. GAO linked much of that record to weak contract planning and oversight. Firms were hired fast, with thin checks on price and performance. Past GAO reports urged tighter contract management, and DOD generally agreed with those calls. The testimony argues that continued progress depends on fixing how contracts are awarded and watched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-120t:
Uneven disability decisions at the Department of Veterans Affairs are discussed in GAO-06-120T, testimony from October 2005. GAO has long reported wide gaps between states in average payments per disabled veteran. In 2002 it found gaps as large as 63 percent. Such gaps raise doubts about whether like cases get like answers. In 2003 GAO placed VA disability programs on its high-risk list, partly over this concern.

Claims staff must use judgment, since ratings rest on medical criteria with broad bands. GAO urged VA to track how that judgment drives variation across its 57 regional offices. One test case involved joint and spine claims. Medical centers supply the exam reports that offices rely on. The share of reports with all required facts ranged from 57 to 92 percent across centers. VA has made real progress on those reports, GAO said. Still, routine monitoring is needed to keep decisions consistent.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-170t:
The Army National Guard's strained role is the subject of GAO-06-170T, testimony presented on October 20, 2005. Since September 2001 the Guard has seen its largest call-up since World War II. Over 30 percent of Army forces in Iraq are Guard members. Guard units also answer homeland security calls and natural disasters. GAO judged whether the Guard can sustain both missions. It weighed the Guard's gear, its changing role, and the Defense Department's plans for its future.

Over 70,000 Guard members serve on federal missions. To field ready units, the Guard shifted people and gear between units. That drained the units left at home. By July 2005 the Guard had sent over 101,000 equipment items overseas. It left over 64,000 more items, worth over $1.2 billion, in theater. The Army cannot account for over half of those items and has no replacement plan. GAO said the Guard's business model is not sustainable and must be reexamined.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-180t:
The Capitol Visitor Center project gets a status check in GAO-06-180T, testimony presented on October 18, 2005. GAO updated Congress on the Architect of the Capitol's work since a hearing held on September 15. Three topics lead: the building schedule, the fire protection system, and project cost and funding. The center was meant to receive Capitol visitors in a secure, purpose-built space. Its build had drawn years of scrutiny over delays and rising cost.

GAO warned that firm answers were not yet at hand. The main builder's September 2005 schedule held large changes the Architect had not yet fully weighed. A cost study by an outside consultant also awaited review. Until the schedule settles, GAO would not give firm completion dates. It also held off updating its November 2004 cost estimate. The testimony shows oversight in midstream, with key facts still being tested.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-220t:
The tax-free status of credit unions is debated in GAO-06-220T, testimony presented on November 3, 2005. Unlike banks, credit unions pay no federal corporate income tax. Law and rule changes have widened what credit unions may do and whom they may serve. The lines between them and banks have blurred. The House Ways and Means Committee asked GAO to trace the roots of the exemption. It also asked for the cases for and against taxing them, and a revenue estimate if the break ended.

GAO checked how far credit union services differ from those of like-sized banks. It asked whether they still serve low- and moderate-income people in a special way. It also reviewed what credit unions must report on executive pay and internal controls. The testimony feeds a long policy fight. Banks call the break unfair; credit unions call it core to their member-owned model.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-370t:
Coal miners' safety plans are only as strong as the review behind them. Testimony GAO-06-370T, dated January 23, 2006, presents GAO findings on the Mine Safety and Health Administration. A Senate panel asked GAO to submit the statement for the record. It draws on GAO's 2003 report on mine safety oversight.

GAO looked at how the agency reviews and approves key mine plans. It also studied inspections and accident investigations. The question was how well those steps protect underground coal miners. The testimony says the programs could be strengthened. Readers get findings on plan review, checks in mines, and follow-up after accidents. The record ties each step to miner health.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-420t:
Home heating bills jumped as wholesale gas prices more than doubled. In testimony GAO-06-420T (February 13, 2006), GAO explains natural gas prices and effects on consumers. In early December 2005, wholesale prices topped $15 per million BTUs. That was seven times the prices common in the 1990s. Homes heating with gas were expected to pay 35 percent more that winter.

GAO sets out the factors pushing prices up. It shows how higher prices hit consumers. It also names the roles federal agencies play in keeping the market fair and informed. The testimony updates GAO work from 2002 with new data. Readers get causes and consumer effects together.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-440t:
A new visitor center under the Capitol kept slipping on time and cost. Testimony GAO-06-440T, given February 15, 2006, gives a risk-based check on the Capitol Visitor Center. GAO spoke to a Senate appropriations panel. The panel had held a hearing on the project on November 16, 2005. GAO assessed risks in the Architect of the Capitol's December 2005 schedule.

GAO offered its own estimate of when the center could open to the public. It also reviewed project costs and funding. It weighed how schedule problems since the hearing could affect cost. Readers get an independent view of a major building project. The focus is risk, not design.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-550t:
A nuclear waste site in Nevada must prove its work is done right. Delivered April 25, 2006, testimony GAO-06-550T covers the Yucca Mountain repository. The Energy Department seeks a license to build the site. The project began in the 1980s and has faced long delays. In 2004, GAO warned that quality assurance problems could delay it further. In 2005, employee e-mails suggesting such problems came to light. The statement sums up a March 2006 GAO report.

GAO gives the history of the quality problems. It tracks the department's handling of them since 2004. It names challenges that remain. Quality assurance guards public health and the environment, the statement stresses.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-600t:
This statement takes the international aid study to a hearing on the same day. Testimony GAO-06-600T, dated April 6, 2006, covers international assistance after Hurricane Katrina. Countries and organizations donated cash and in-kind help to the United States. Foreign military help was included. The State Department coordinates all offers of foreign assistance. The Federal Emergency Management Agency accepts help and coordinates its distribution. GAO's testimony follows its companion report of the same date.

GAO covers the amount and use of donated cash from abroad. It checks policies for in-kind help as well. Policies and procedures are needed to ensure proper use and accountability, GAO said. Readers get the testimony version of the findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-610t:
Unmanned aircraft systems used by the armed forces are covered in GAO-06-610T, testimony dated April 6, 2006. As of February 2006, the Department of Defense had more than 3,000 unmanned aircraft. About 2,000 of them were supporting operations in Iraq. The 2006 defense review called for much more spending on these systems in the years ahead.

GAO reported both combat successes and hard problems, such as keeping the aircraft safe and useful in crowded skies. GAO said joint planning and oversight across the services were still weak. GAO also assessed the Global Hawk and Predator programs and the lessons they held for a planned joint combat system. Better planning and buying strategies, GAO said, could cut cost and risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-660t:
Export promotion teamwork across agencies is the topic of GAO-06-660T, testimony GAO presented on April 26, 2006. Congress set up the Trade Promotion Coordinating Committee in 1992 to unify export promotion work. Member agencies offer training, market data, advocacy, and trade finance to United States firms, mainly small and mid-sized ones. Together they held $1.5 billion in budget authority for export programs in fiscal year 2006.

GAO said the committee had taken steps to improve coordination, but its role remained limited. Its yearly strategies gave little guidance for export programs. Reported budget authority had declined, though the data had gaps. GAO also found that weak data hampered judging how well small exporters were served. The testimony shows the limits of coordination without clear authority.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-740t:
Telework in emergency plans is the topic of GAO-06-740T, testimony GAO presented on May 11, 2006. Continuity plans must keep vital government services running during a disaster. Federal guidance tells agencies to weigh telework for key staff who cannot reach an office. GAO surveyed agencies on how their plans use telework. GAO compared the answers with its earlier survey work.

GAO found that more agencies planned for essential staff to telework than before. Nine of the 23 agencies said some essential team members were expected to telework in an emergency. Yet few agencies documented the preparations needed to make that work. Only one agency documented that it had told its teleworkers what to expect. GAO urged better planning so telework is ready when a crisis hits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-760t:
Screening of veterans' health workers is updated in GAO-06-760T, testimony GAO presented on June 15, 2006. In March 2004, GAO urged the Department of Veterans Affairs to improve how it screens health care practitioners. Weak screening can let unqualified or barred staff treat veterans. GAO returned to check the steps the department had taken. GAO also reviewed how the department credentials doctors and grants them clinical privileges.

GAO said the department had partly put each of the four 2004 recommendations into practice. Gaps still remained in its screening requirements. For one recommendation, checks of all state licenses and national certificates covered only some practitioner groups. Physician privileging practices also needed work. GAO concluded that patient safety could be enhanced by closing these gaps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-790t:
Evacuating the frail during hurricanes is the focus of GAO-06-790T, testimony presented on May 18, 2006. Hurricane Katrina forced the evacuation of hospital patients, nursing home residents, and people who lack transport. These vulnerable groups cannot simply drive away from a storm. GAO shared early observations on how such evacuations work and where they strain. The testimony draws on the Katrina experience and other disasters.

GAO found that hospital and nursing home leaders face hard choices. They must decide whether to evacuate at all, and then find transport for patients who need special care. State and local orders can exempt health facilities, leaving the call to administrators. A late or wrong call can trap patients in danger. GAO urged better planning for the most fragile residents.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-800t:
Defense buying reform is the theme of GAO-06-800T, testimony GAO presented on September 7, 2006. Defense spending on goods and services had grown since fiscal year 2000 to well over $250 billion a year. Wide deficits made wise spending more urgent. War fighters still needed the right gear at the best value. GAO set out how contracting could deliver better outcomes for troops and taxpayers alike.

GAO walked through recent contracting trends across the department. It stressed sound business deals as the base of good buying. Competition and sound pricing, GAO said, must anchor contract awards. Fees should reward real results, and oversight must follow the work after award. The testimony collects GAO's core buying lessons in one place. It is a compact guide to a huge spending system.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-840t:
Regional gaps in environmental enforcement fill GAO-06-840T, testimony GAO gave on June 28, 2006. The Environmental Protection Agency polices the nation's green laws through its enforcement office. That office sets policy, while the agency's 10 regional offices carry out most enforcement. GAO reported on the effort to improve those activities and make them more consistent. The testimony builds on earlier GAO work under the Clean Water Act and Clean Air Act.

GAO said the regions vary substantially in the actions they take. The differences show up in the very indicators headquarters uses to watch performance. Inspection counts at regulated facilities are one such marker. Penalty amounts are another. Wide swings suggest that a firm's treatment may depend on its region. The testimony presses the agency to even out its enforcement hand.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-900t:
Superfund cleanups, and the safeguards left behind at waste sites, are the subject of GAO testimony GAO-06-900T, dated June 15, 2006. Polluters should bear cleanup costs under the program. Some no longer exist, though, and many sites keep waste in place under land or water use limits.

The testimony sums up two earlier GAO reports, from August 2005 and January 2005. GAO urged a financial promise rule for firms that handle hazardous goods. It also urged closer watch on controls at sites, and exact records of their state. Readers learn how long-term site safety rests on checks that can fade.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-910t:
Early effects of a new transport law on transit aid form the core of GAO testimony GAO-06-910T, dated June 27, 2006. The law, known as SAFETEA-LU, set over $52 billion for federal transit programs. It added new programs and changed old ones, among them New Starts and Job Access and Reverse Commute.

Those two programs held $8.6 billion in backing. GAO gave early findings on changes to each, based on talks with transit officials, project backers, and trade groups. It also flagged points to watch as the Federal Transit Administration put the law into practice. The testimony is a progress note, not a final grade.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-930t:
Growth in geothermal energy, and what blocks it, is the topic of GAO testimony GAO-06-930T, dated July 11, 2006. Heat from the earth can make power in any weather. Fossil fuels still gave about 86 percent of U.S. energy use at the time.

GAO told the Senate that current geothermal growth is limited. It set out the many hurdles builders face on federal lands. It traced steps by federal, state, and local bodies to meet those hurdles. It also warned that payments of geothermal royalties would change sharply. The testimony argues that wider use hangs on clearing those blocks, not on the resource itself.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-940t:
Border screening is tested again in GAO testimony GAO-06-940T, dated July 7, 2006, a companion to the statement given two days before. GAO agents drove radioactive sources toward U.S. ports of entry. Customs and Border Protection inspectors staff those ports, the first line for travelers and goods.

The agents crossed with the sources at two sites. GAO set out whether port monitors sensed the load, and how inspectors acted at each stop. It pointed readers to its study report, GAO-06-545R, for the full record. The short statement keeps its focus tight: one covert test, two crossings, and what they reveal about daily border checks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1050t:
Medicare should pay one bundled rate for kidney failure care, GAO states in a statement for the record, GAO-07-1050T, dated June 26, 2007. People with end-stage renal disease get dialysis to clear their blood. They also get drugs for ills tied to kidney loss, such as low blood counts and low calcium.

At the time, drugs were paid apart from the dialysis rate. GAO urged that all items and services join one bundled rate, as soon as fair. Full grounds sit in its report from a December 6, 2006 hearing. The statement sums up that case, and facts other witnesses gave at the hearing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1090t:
Tax-exempt groups owe close to $1 billion in payroll and other taxes, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1090T, dated July 24, 2007. As of September 2006, nearly 1.8 million bodies held tax-exempt status. They pay no income tax, but must still send in tax withheld from staff wages, plus Social Security and Medicare sums.

Past GAO work found unpaid taxes among contractors, Medicare providers, and campaign charities. GAO audited exempt groups at a House member's request, with 25 case studies. It asked how much tax is unpaid, if case groups or their chiefs engaged in abuse, and if tax debtors got federal grants. Data came from the tax agency and 3 grant systems.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1100t:
Missing tech gear at veterans sites is the topic of GAO testimony GAO-07-1100T, dated July 24, 2007. In July 2004 GAO found six medical centers with weak property lists. Fewer than half the items it picked for testing could be found. Most missing items were tech gear.

With laptop thefts and data breaches fresh in mind, GAO tested four sites. It weighed the risk of theft, loss, or misuse of tech gear there. It checked if disposal steps guard gear on its way out. It asked what agency chiefs have done on the flaws found. Weak control and poor answerability, the title states, leave gear exposed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1140t:
Fair exposure to environmental risk needs clear yardsticks, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1140T, dated July 25, 2007. A 1994 order told agencies to guard minority and low-income groups from outsize environmental harm. Studies show those groups do bear more air pollution and health risk.

GAO summed up its July 2005 report, GAO-05-289, on three clean air rules. That work found flaws in how the Environmental Protection Agency weighs such fairness early in rule writing. GAO set out its advice, and the agency's August 24, 2006 reply. It added fresh facts on agency steps since. Yardsticks that can be measured, GAO said, are needed to gauge headway.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1150t:
Capitol utility tunnels, and the hazards inside them, are updated in GAO testimony GAO-07-1150T, dated August 1, 2007. The Architect of the Capitol runs five walkable tunnels with steam and chilled water pipes. They heat and cool the Capitol and over 20 nearby buildings.

Workers and a workplace safety office raised alarms on tunnel state. In January 2006 citations flagged a possible asbestos risk and heat stress. A February 2006 complaint added falling concrete, weak contact systems, and poor escape exits. Some points date back to 1999. In June 2007 the two sides settled, with fixes due within 5 years. GAO set out the projects, schedule, and costs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1220t:
Congress set 18 benchmarks to judge whether Iraq's government was making progress. GAO delivered testimony GAO-07-1220T on September 4, 2007, reporting its rating of each one. The benchmarks covered laws, security, basic services, and the economy. They came from a 2007 appropriations act that required GAO to report. GAO reviewed U.S. and Iraqi records and spoke with officials in both countries.

As of August 30, 2007, Iraq had met 3 benchmarks and partly met 4 more. It had not met the other 11. Key laws on sharing oil wealth and on former Ba'ath party members had stalled. GAO said it was unclear whether the Baghdad security plan had cut sectarian violence. It urged clearer reporting on Iraqi laws, violence trends, and the readiness of Iraqi forces.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1230t:
A unity deal among Iraq's top leaders in late August 2007 raised hopes for reconciliation. Days later, on September 7, 2007, GAO published testimony GAO-07-1230T on Iraq's benchmark record. The statement scores the 18 benchmarks Congress wrote into a 2007 funding act. GAO based its ratings on field visits and talks with U.S. and Iraqi officials. Ambassador Ryan Crocker and General David H. Petraeus were among those interviewed.

GAO rated 3 benchmarks met and 4 partly met, with 11 not met. The Unity Accord covered draft de-Ba'athification and provincial powers laws. It also set a path to free some Sunni detainees held without charges. But GAO said fighting among Shi'a factions weakened the governing coalition further. On security, it found no clear proof that violence had fallen under the Baghdad plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1240t:
The Department of Homeland Security was four years old, and Congress wanted a progress report. In GAO-07-1240T, dated September 18, 2007, GAO graded that progress. The testimony rests on GAO's August 2007 report on the department. It covers 14 mission and management areas, from border security to finance. GAO has called the department's creation one of the largest federal reorganizations in decades.

GAO found more progress on plans than on putting those plans into practice. In border security, the department had a multiyear strategy for illegal crossings. Yet work to carry out that strategy was still at an early stage. Emergency response showed the same pattern under the National Incident Management System. GAO noted that large mergers often take 5 to 7 years to succeed. Even so, it said much hard work remained across the department.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1250t:
The Everglades now cover about half the ground they once did. In testimony GAO-07-1250T, dated September 19, 2007, GAO reported on the huge effort to restore South Florida's ecosystem. The plan spans about 18,000 square miles and 222 projects. It was set in 2000 and was expected to take at least 40 years. The price tag then stood at $15.4 billion. GAO drew on its May 2007 report for the statement.

GAO said some restoration progress was real, but the effort faced big delays. Only 43 of the 222 projects had been completed. Many finished projects improved water quality or bought land for habitat. The projects not yet started were mostly the core restoration plan works. Those are the ones most vital to the health of Everglades National Park. GAO also found that total costs had climbed as schedules slipped.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-370t:
Two farm conservation programs pay farmers for green practices, but the money flow needs tighter steering. GAO summed up its findings in testimony GAO-07-370T on January 17, 2007. The statement draws on recent reports about both programs. One program shares costs for conservation work. The other pays for ongoing stewardship. GAO checked how funds reach states. It checked performance tracking and duplicate payments.

The funding formula lacks a clear link to green benefit, GAO reported. It blends 31 factors with no written rationale. Some factor data are old or doubtful. Funds may miss the states with the worst farm pollution. Long-term outcome measures are in development. They could sharpen the formula later. Duplicate payments slip through as well. Some farmers drew both programs for the same practice. No full process exists to catch the overlap. GAO urged better program management.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-390t:
Rail accidents per mile have stalled after decades of improvement, and the safety agency is retargeting its work. GAO described the shift in testimony GAO-07-390T on January 30, 2007. The statement rests on GAO's January 26, 2007 report. A South Carolina wreck frames the stakes. It killed 9 people and injured 292 in Graniteville. The rail agency sets standards and inspects for compliance. GAO judged how it picks its targets.

The agency's 2005 action plan targets the two top crash causes, GAO said. They are human error and defective track. Inspection planning now follows risk more closely. But the agency cannot show what its oversight achieves. It lacks measures for inspection and enforcement results. It has not evaluated its enforcement program. GAO recommended building both. The transport department gave no overall view on the draft report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-400t: Health IT was racing ahead of privacy in 2007, and GAO's briefing says a comprehensive privacy approach was needed for the national effort. The testimony demands the safeguards. The findings warn that the digital chart should not become a public record. The patients' secrets needed locks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-460t: The Coast Guard's Deepwater program kept struggling in 2007, and GAO's briefing reviews the management fixes and operational challenges. The testimony takes stock. The findings warn that the fleet of the future needed steadier hands. The cutters could not wait for competence.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-490t: The FAA faced a turbulent 2008 in 2007, and GAO's briefing lays out the challenges awaiting the agency in the fiscal year ahead. The testimony previews the storms. The findings warn that the skies' guardian was flying into headwinds. The turbulence was already on the radar.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-530t: Retirement was shifting to the 401(k) in 2007, and GAO's briefing says workers needed better information on the fees eating their savings. The testimony targets the hidden costs. The findings warn that the do-it-yourself pension had do-it-yourself dangers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-550t: Advanced energy tech faced a valley of death in 2007, and GAO's briefing names the key challenges to developing and deploying it. The testimony maps the obstacles. The findings warn that the breakthroughs would die in the lab without a bridge to the market.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-580t: The scariest nuclear material needed guarding first in 2007, and GAO's briefing says focusing on the highest-priority radiological sources would sharpen the Energy Department's work. The testimony sets the priorities clearly. The findings argue for guarding the worst stuff first.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-630t: Privacy was the casualty the security state kept forgetting in 2007, and GAO's briefing says the concerns needed steady attention as programs grew. The testimony keeps the flag raised high. The findings argue that safety bought with liberty needs a receipt, or the price is hidden.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-700t: The watchdog was being shut out in 2007 — GAO's briefing tells Congress about the fight to pry information from Homeland Security. The testimony defends the auditor's right to see the files. The findings stand on a simple principle: oversight cannot do its job blindfolded by the agency it oversees.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-710t: The piracy fight needed a real general in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the national plan to stop fakes wanted stronger leadership and clear answers. The testimony demands a true commander. The findings argue that fake goods need a real strategy to beat them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-720t: Tax season 2007 got its interim report card — GAO's briefing updates the paid-preparer probe and the IRS's modernization drive. The testimony checks the filing numbers. The findings keep score on who did your taxes right this year, and who did not.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-730t: Space buying needed to grow up in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the best practices for acquisitions had to spread and stick across programs. The testimony demands wider adoption at every level. The findings' hope is plain: rockets bought right tend to fly right, and rockets bought wrong do not.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-760t: Climate risk was an insurer's time bomb in 2007 — GAO's briefing repeats the warning on the financial exposure looming ahead. The testimony prices the decades of peril in hard numbers. The findings' message: the storms of tomorrow are priced today, or paid for in full later.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-820t: Climate change was an insurer's nightmare in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the financial risks to public and private insurers could run huge in the decades ahead. The testimony prices the peril. The findings warn that the storms would send bills, not just winds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-840t: A gas-tanker disaster at sea haunted planners in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the fallout of an LNG spill needed clearer spelling out. The testimony demands the worst-case math. The findings argue that ports should know the price of the peril.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-850t: Foster kids with the toughest needs were falling through in 2007 — GAO's briefing says more federal action could help states serve them. The testimony presses for the hard cases. The findings argue that the system must stretch for the children it finds hardest to place.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-890t: Hiring private debt collectors split taxpayers in 2007 — GAO's briefing measures what people thought of the IRS's collection contractors. The testimony polls the public mood on for-profit dunning. The findings capture the unease of getting a collection call from a company with a quota.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-910t: The polar weather eyes were being rebuilt in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the satellite restructuring was underway, with big risks riding along. The testimony tracks the high-stakes overhaul in detail. The findings warn that the planet's forecasters were flying on aging wings.
